meaningMnemonic: He's a creeper and he's Four-T (forty). If someone like this creeps on you, they're just a bully . When you get to forty you aren't supposed to creep on people anymore. You bully. You jerk.

Imagine this in your mouth. It's one tooth that sticks out more than any other. It's your fang . Can you see this sticking out of a wolf mouth instead? Try that if you can't picture yourself with a fang this cool.
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means guy .
There's a door over the bookcase. That makes this a library !
This radical is the same as the kanji. It means line up .

See how there’s a lid on top of the treasure chest? That’s because the whole thing is a rocket which contains all the necessary items (treasures) to live in outer space. The bottom part of the radical shows you that this is a top secret project, though, so keep this private in your own head.

This radical means stomach , since it kind of looks like one. See the big stomach sitting on top of some intestines that snake downwards? Just keep in mind this radical is specifically for the stomach, and the stomach only — not all the other stuff attached to it. You could also remember it with a mnemonic: To eat a rice paddy the size of the moon, you'd need a pretty impressive stomach. Every doctor and scientist in the world would probably be jostling to get a look at your incredible stomach and see how you managed to fit a moon-sized rice paddy into it.

There's a mountain coming out of the ground that you want to climb, but your forehead needs a towel for all your sweat. You don't have a towel, so you take off your belt and tie it around your forehead. Hints The belt is easy to tighten and it catches all the sweat before it can fall into your eyes. It isn't quite as absorbent as a towel though.
readingMnemonic: The belt isn't absorbent enough, so you wrap it in your tie ( たい ) and then tie the whole thing around your forehead again. Hints It works! Your belt tied in a tie is the perfect invention!

meaningMnemonic: The canopy guy is a guy who stands in the corridor trying to sell people canopies. Hints You walk through this corridor every day, and the canopy guy always accosts you with canopy sales. You wish there was another corridor you could take, but it's the only way to get where you want to go.
readingMnemonic: You take the corridor , but this time the canopy guy is gone. In his place is a new salesman. This one is trying to sell you roe ( ろう ). Hints The roe salesman in the corridor is worse than the canopy salesman. They're both insistent, but the roe salesman smells bad.

meaningMnemonic: The rocket turkey has several points which will detach during takeoff. Hints Imagine the rocket turkey taking off. Just like a regular rocket, as it goes up, used pieces of the turkey rocket detach and fall back to the ground.
readingMnemonic: When the rocket turkey parts detach , they fall to the ground onto a bed of ree ds ( り ). Hints The reeds catch on fire - probably best not to fire off turkey rockets so close to these fields of reeds. Imagine the launch site completely surrounded by reeds.

meaningMnemonic: You loiter around a tombstone to measure its diameter . You’re doing this to each tombstone, and if you loiter around long enough, you’ll soon know the diameter of every tombstone. Hints Imagine loitering around a tombstone. You're leaning on it. You're staring at nothing. Oh, and you're also measuring its diameter.
readingMnemonic: You need to know the diameter of each tombstone so you can make ca kes ( けい ) for each one. But the cakes can't be wider than the tombstones, or they'll flop off onto the ground. Hints These carefully measured tombstone-diameter cakes are your special way of saying thanks to the ghosts for letting you loiter around their graves.

meaningMnemonic: You see a bully take an insect and dissolve it in some acid. Bullies are messed up, mean people. They do awful things that normal kids and people wouldn't do... like dissolve a living creature. Hints Actually... try to forget this one. Don't think about a bully dissolving things in acid. Think happy thoughts. Like... the bully getting dissolved instead and all the little insects coming back to life and being happy.
readingMnemonic: The only bullies heartless enough to dissolve insects like this are you ths ( ゆう ). Do you really think an adult would melt a harmless critter? No. Only inexperienced youths could be so cruel. Hints When you first read this and you pictured the bully dissolving the insect, you pictured them as a youth, right? See? It makes complete sense.

meaningMnemonic: You have some dirt next to a pool that has an extra drop of water in it because you need them to be equal . If there's too much dirt outside the pool and not enough water inside, it's gonna look weird. We can't have that. Hints Imagine seeing a pool that isn't equal. It's like a tiny kiddy pool with an inch of water. And it's surrounded by mounds of dirt. No no no, this won't do—add more water to make them equal.
readingMnemonic: You spend a few hours making sure the water-to-dirt ratio is perfectly equal , not for yourself, but because the Kin g ( きん ) of England told you to. You may agree that equality is important, but it's the King's responsibility to keep things that way. Which is why he ordered you, small peon, to do the equalizing work for him. Hints Okay, so the existence of a king kind of makes things not, well, equal, for all people. But at least aesthetically everything will be!

meaningMnemonic: You put a lid on a dish you're cooking, made up of the mouth s and forehead s of a pig . This is truly an exceptional dish you are cooking up. Hints Mix those pig mouths and foreheads in your pot. Think of how exceptional your soup looks.
readingMnemonic: Exceptional pig mouth forehead soup is a favorite of Grandpa ごう いち . You see him sniffing around your window, then he knocks and waves. Hints "Can I have some of your exceptional soup?" Grandpa ごういち asks. "It smells so swell."

meaningMnemonic: The building s are at a surplus . Because of that, we will need to exclude some of them from our future plans. Also, we'll need to remove some buildings too. Hints Say you're looking at a map of the city, with all the buildings laid out on it. There are too many, so you start marking which ones to exclude from the building plans. You also remove some buildings from the map all together.
readingMnemonic: Working with you on this project to exclude buildings from the plan, as well as remove buildings that already exist is little Jo -Anne ( じょ ). Hints She's pointing out buildings to exclude / remove with great ferocity. "Remove this one. Exclude this one. Oh, and remove this one too."

meaningMnemonic: You want to change your shellfish into freight so you can transport it. That means packing them up into giant freight containers. Hints Imagine changing your shellfish from loose, wet form, to solid freight form. It's actually a lot of hard work.
readingMnemonic: To move this freight , you need a ca r ( か ). You strap all of the freight containers to the top of your car, stacked nice and high and precarious, so you can move it. Hints Picture all of this freight stacked on top of your car. As you drive the car, every turn you make feels slow and heavy from the freight weight.

meaningMnemonic: A child shares his lineage with a grandchild . The child passes his lineage down to his child and then that child’s child is the grandchild and between them all a lineage is shared. Hints Look at this family tree. See the child, and then the grandchild. Trace the lineage with your finger as you observe.
readingMnemonic: The son ( そん ) of a son is a grandchild . In this case, a grandson. Easy. Hints Just remember that a son is all you really want. You need a son to carry on the family name and the lineage. So make sure that your child and your grandchild are both sons.

meaningMnemonic: Inside your greenhouse there's a mound of dirt which appears to be someone's grave . When you dig into it, you discover that it's an entire tomb , with doors and passages and everything! Hints Why would someone put a grave in a greenhouse? Is this one of those "green burials" everyone's talking about these days? Having the whole tomb complex seems a tad counterproductive, though…
readingMnemonic: You pry open the grave inside the inner chamber of the tomb , and are shocked to find the mummified body of Bo bo ( ぼ ) the Clown staring back at you! How terrifying! Hints You watch in horror as Bobo raises his arms and slowly rises from his grave. "At last, I have awoken from my slumber… Prepare yourselves, mortals — Bobo's taking reservations for birthday parties again!"

meaningMnemonic: You poop twice on a sleeping drunkard person and you find yourself wondering how many more times you can poop on them and wonder how much they can take before they realize what’s going on. Hints You’ve already pooped twice on this drunkard, how many more times can you do it? How much do you think this person can take? Just imagine yourself doing this.
readingMnemonic: As you continue thinking about how much poop this drunkard can take and how many more poops you can drop on him, he begins to wake up. Quickly, you eke ( いく ) out one last poop before you scurry away. You eke that poop out just in time to make your escape. Hints Imagine yourself as you eke out that last poop. Really concentrate on eking it out so you can get away in time. Flex your butt muscles for added effect.

meaningMnemonic: Wolverine is doing a construction job and using his mouth to take measurement s, so he knows how many folks he needs to inquire with about helping him. Using the mouth is a strange way to take measurements, but that's just how Wolverine does things. Once he measures it all out, he'll know how many construction workers he needs to inquire with about working for him. Hints Imagine Wolverine going around, measuring the construction site with his mouth. Look at him with his mouth wide open, wandering around the site deep in thought. What a weirdo.
readingMnemonic: Another thing Wolverine has to inquire about is jean s ( じん ). He wants to make sure everyone on the construction site has good-fitting jeans to work in, so he inquires with them about their jean measurements. Hints Imagine Wolverine handing you some new jeans at the construction site. Um, they're kind of all ripped up? Turns out that's just the style he likes. You'll be so fashionable now! Just like good old '90s Wolvie.

meaningMnemonic: Bring thread to the library to knit . Libraries are quiet and generally pretty empty nowadays, so it's the perfect place to relax and do some knitting. Of course, if you find thread lying around in a library you know what to do now. Hints Picture yourself sitting on a rocking chair in the library knitting away. It's quiet and peaceful and the light is warming you just right. Ahh, bliss!
readingMnemonic: You need to come to the library to knit because if you try to do it at home all your hen s ( へん ) will try to eat the thread. Hens love eating things that look like worms, like hay, string, and thread. So it's important to get far away from them before you start to knit. Hints Imagine the granny or grampy you are (and must be to have hens and want to knit in peace in a library). You're tired of these hens eating your thread while you try to knit sweaters for all your grandbabies so you come to the library.

meaningMnemonic: A building made from a womb must be placed upon the land . Hints Why must it be placed upon the land? If it were put in water, it would dissolve too quickly. So, you put your womb building on the land, instead.
readingMnemonic: The land around your womb building will, unfortunately, reek ( りく ) though. Hints It's made of biological materials, so of course it will reek.

meaningMnemonic: Put your fingers to your forehead and stand your legs high up in a tree if you want to look for something. After all, shielding your eyes and getting up high is the best way to look for something, isn’t it? Hints Imagine it's like a quest from a book or game. What are you looking for? Maybe a powerful sword, or a lost princess. Picture it in your mind, this thing you're looking for.
readingMnemonic: You look for it for so long that you can't help getting a tan ( たん ). I mean, you're up some tree, shielding your eyes from the sun as you look for that thing, and it's been hours, days? Of course you're going to get a tan. Hints Feel the sun's rays on your skin as you search and search and search. Watch as your skin gets darker, crispier, and — hmm — starts smelling like cooked meat. Now that's a good tan.

meaningMnemonic: See that gold man oversee ing everyone? He's a model human. His goldenness is a sign of how exemplary he is, and he's overseeing all of us flawed, regular folks to try to help us get on his level. Hints Imagine this golden man standing on a raised platform, looking down at you judgmentally with his arms crossed. You mutter curses at him under your breath, but really you're just jealous you're not a model human like him.
readingMnemonic: As you look closer at the golden model human, you realize he's actually Genghis Khan ( かん )! No wonder he's covered in gold and overseeing everyone — he's the greatest conqueror in history! Hints Hold on a sec — didn't Genghis Khan kill a bunch of people and father like a thousand kids? He doesn't seem like such a model person to you, but, hey, you don't make the rules around here — Genghis Khan does.

meaningMnemonic: A tsunami came in and buried your flag so now you have to use a spoon and dig it out of the mud . Hints Imagine using a spoon to dig your flag outta all this mud. So much mud! Feel its cold, soiled wetness on your hands as you dig away.
readingMnemonic: You may know of Dora the Explorer. But have you heard about her dirty, mud dy brother, Doro ( どろ )? They're like a team. And because of all the exploring he does, Doro is always covered in mud. Hints Imagine them working together — Dora and Doro, the Muddy Explorers! Who knows why she's able to stay clean, while Doro gets so muddy…

meaningMnemonic: Birds use grass and fruit to make their nest s. Hints Picture a cute little nest with a family of birds in it. It looks like it was woven together with bits of grass and strawberries, so it smells delicious too.
readingMnemonic: The bottom of the nest also seems to be padded with someone's su it ( す ). Did... did this bird attack a human for this?! Hints Picture the nest, made of grass, fruit, and the suit of the angry salaryman who's shouting below the tree, and missing the top half of his suit.

meaningMnemonic: You line up your body with the sun and everything looks normal .  The sun is lined up behind you, and you’re looking at all the things the sun has lit up. Everything looks normal. Hints Gaze out in a line from the sun as you observe the world. Everything is very normal looking and comforting.
readingMnemonic: Soon you see something that doesn’t look so normal . It’s a foo l ( ふ ), a jester. Dressed all in fool’s garb, this fool is dancing up towards you with a ridiculously unsettling grin on his face. Hints Imagine this creepy looking fool as he approaches. He’s kind of freaking you out. Feel very uncomfortable as you continue looking at this fool.

meaningMnemonic: A woman with direction will have things obstruct her path. It's a sad fact that it's still a man's world out there! Hints Picture this woman with direction, knocking down obstruction after obstruction on her path to success.
readingMnemonic: This woman is truly magnificent. Some compare her to a bow ling ( ぼう ) ball, because of how she knocks down the obstructions in her path like bowling pins. Hints Now imagine that she actually is a bowling ball. Watch her roll down the bowling lane and smash all those stupid pins!

meaningMnemonic: A tree in spring that's nice and dry will make a good pole or rod . Break it out of the ground and give it a swing to see what a nice, sturdy stick it is! Hints Use this pole to hang your towels or curtains. Ooh, use it to pole vault!
readingMnemonic: After much deliberation, you decide to use this pole to go bow ling ( ぼう ). It's a pretty long pole, so you can just stand at the top of the lane and directly poke the bowling pins with it. Hints Imagine all the irritated glares you get as you use your pole to cheat your way through several games of bowling. That's against the rules, buddy!

meaningMnemonic: If you grind rice , every part of it, eventually it will become a fine powder . You can then use this rice powder as a part to create some other dish. Some kind of cake, perhaps. Hints Imagine yourself grinding this rice into a powder. Hear the scrape of the rice on stone as you grind it down to the finest powder.
readingMnemonic: Actually, grinding the rice down to a powder is super fun ( ふん ). It’s so fun you don’t want to stop! AH HAHAHAHA! RICE POWDER! SO FUN! Hints Okay, we got a little carried away there. Just keep in mind how fun this is. Make sure you say fun with a little bit of a Scottish accent. You know what they say, Scots have more fun!

meaningMnemonic: There's a root where your fang previously was. Your fang isn't there anymore, you ripped it out. Hints Look at the root where your fang previously was. Previously, when you were young, you had a lot of nice fangs but they're all rotting as you get older and you pull them out.
readingMnemonic: To remember the beautiful fangs you previously had, you keep all of the ones you pull out in a box you lock with a key ( き ). Hints Previously you didn't have a key, but now you do to keep your old fangs safe.

meaningMnemonic: You request that winter rescue you from the warmth of the other seasons. Hints It's so hot. You hate it. You really hope winter will get your request and come early to rescue you.
readingMnemonic: You get a note in the mail from winter! This is it, you're going to be rescued! You open the note and it says, "I have rescue d you with this cu cumber ( きゅう )." A cucumber falls out of the note. Hints This cucumber is supposed to be cool and refreshing enough to rescue you from the heat. I guess it was too much to expect winter to come early just for you. At least cucumbers are yummy.

meaningMnemonic: A leader of (odd-looking) lion s puts a drop of magic liquid on his face to look like a person who resemble s someone else. The leader of lions is going incognito, so he needs to resemble a person who is not himself. He takes this drop of powerful face paint and transforms. Hints Watch this leader as the transformation takes place. Now he doesn’t resemble anything like the leader he used to be. He doesn’t look like the same person. Watch him morph in your head.
readingMnemonic: Now he resemble s an even greater leader, and all the lions get down on one knee ( に ) to pay their respects. (Note that we recently changed this kanji's main reading from ね to に , because ね is an irregular reading.) Hints See all the odd-looking lions respectfully getting down on one knee? They look even odder now.

meaningMnemonic: On your roof is a scarecrow because you're rich . You want to scare away all the poor, non-rich people so you put a scarecrow on your roof. Hints Imagine looking up at the roof at this scarecrow. There's a sign around its neck that says, "Rich people welcome." Ah, you're safe. Time to go to bed!
readingMnemonic: You wake up the next morning and all of your rich es have been stolen! You call the police and they call you a foo l ( ふ )! Pardon me?! "You basically put an advertisement on your roof telling everyone you're rich. Of course you got robbed, you fool." Hints You poor sad, no longer rich fool.

meaningMnemonic: If you play blackjack on the moon in the winter , your cards will scatter everywhere. The cards scatter because the gravity is so weak on the moon, so the blackjack game is prone to disaster. Hints Imagine playing blackjack on the moon where even the slightest move causes the cards to scatter about. Watch them float along. It’s very frustrating to play this way.
readingMnemonic: You are playing blackjack with San ta-san ( さん ). Santa-san is doing his best to use his Christmas magic to prevent the scatter of cards, but it’s not working out so well. Good effort, Santa-san. Hints Imagine yourself next to Santa-san as he tries to prevent the cards from scattering. Look at the expression of concentration on Santa-san’s face as he tries to prevent the scatter.

meaningMnemonic: Flowers growing out of a rice paddy into the shape of a cross are really showy flower s. Hints Picture these showy flowers growing straight up and out of the middle of the rice paddy, into the shape of a giant cross.
readingMnemonic: These flower s are too showy . You hate them. You hate these showy flowers so much you run them over with your ca r ( か )! Hints Imagine how the car feels as you ram into the showy flowers. The petals explode and rain everywhere. You turn on your windshield wipers to push them away.

meaningMnemonic: You use your mouth when you see a Chinese person and you sigh . You sigh so loud that it’s practically a roar coming out of your mouth. Chinese people and Chinese things make you sigh because it reminds you of when you stayed in China and it brings up memories. The sigh is a sigh of nostalgia. Hints Let out a long sigh as you recall memories from China and all the Chinese things you saw and did. Oh, sigh.
readingMnemonic: Your favorite Chinese thing to do is tan ( たん ). You can wander around without your shirt on and tan all day. No one will sigh or scoff at you, it’s perfectly acceptable. The Chinese just love to get their tan on. Hints Sigh again as you remember how nice it was to tan everywhere. Picture yourself wandering around some Chinese streets with your shirt off as you soak in the rays and get a tan.

meaningMnemonic: Your leader sticks his toe into a shellfish . You ask him why and he says he wants to spy on it. Hints There’s a hidden camera on his toe and the leader wants to have plenty of secret spy footage to review later.
readingMnemonic: You and the leader review the spy footage and find a single ta ter ( てい ) tot hidden within the shellfish. Together you uncover a huge smuggling ring. Clams, oysters, mussels, you name it! Shellfish of all kinds are using their bodies to sneak tater tots to the undersea world. Hints If it wasn't for your toe spy network, these egregious tater tot crimes would have never reached the light of day.

meaningMnemonic: The radical stomach and the kanji stomach are exactly the same! Hints The kanji that you already know are the easiest ones to stomach.
readingMnemonic: Inside your stomach , you secretly keep an ea gle ( い ) to help you digest things. As one of nature's top predators, an eagle can consume just about any food you throw at it, so it's really handy to have one living in your stomach. Hints Whenever you put food into your stomach, your eagle tears it to shreds with its beak and pre-processes it for you. Sometimes it accidentally pecks you, though, which is a little painful.

meaningMnemonic: If you can write an interesting poem about winter while riding on a horse , I’ll be pretty surprised . It’s hard enough to write a poem as it is, let alone an interesting one. And then you’re riding on a horse and the poem has to be about winter? Heck, I’d be surprised if you didn’t fall off the horse and injure yourself. Hints Imagine trying to write a poem while riding a horse. It’d be really hard to do. I bet you’d be surprised if you managed to do it as well.
readingMnemonic: You might also be surprised to learn that you are to ride this horse all across きょう と . That gives you a time limit. You have until you traverse きょうと to write this poem about winter. Hints Imagine riding through きょうと on a horse. As if that wasn’t difficult enough for poem writing, now you have all the sights and sounds of きょうと to distract you as well.

meaningMnemonic: Wrap your fingers around this broom , because it's time to sweep ! Hints Keep your fingers tightly wrapped around the broom — if you drop it mid-sweep, all that dirt and dust will go flying everywhere and you'll have to start over from scratch.
readingMnemonic: Sweep ing is good for the sou l ( そう ). Every sweep of the broom makes your soul a little more pure. Cleanliness is next to godliness, after all. Hints Feel your soul getting more and more purified as you sweep every inch of your house. Your soul's getting squeaky-clean, and it honestly feels amazing.

meaningMnemonic: You want some flowers so you take your cleat to the side of a tree hoping they'll fall down, but you get a vegetable instead. What? You kick the tree again and another, different vegetable falls out. Hints Now you have two vegetables and no flowers. Do vegetables even grow on trees?
readingMnemonic: You feed these vegetable s (that you didn't even want) to your cy borg ( さい ). It only needs a little though, since its stomach is so thin, so you just make it hold the rest. Hints Picture your cyborg nibbling on the vegetables you cleat-kicked out of this tree. You give all of the things you don't like to your cyborg nowadays. Which is probably why there are so many weird things all over it...

meaningMnemonic: Under the moon while you sit on a cliff , you inject a syringe of tofu right into your vein . Ahh, tofu. You're addicted to it. You sneak out to the cliff at night to get your tofu fix, injecting it straight into your vein. Hints Feel the tofu running through your veins. Feel the tofu goodness spreading all over your body. It's so intense you can even taste a little tofu in your mouth.
readingMnemonic: Eventually, your friends and family find you at the cliff, tripping on tofu. Each and every vein on your body is engorged, pulsating with the effects of tofu. Your friends try and take you home. "You cyan't myake ( みゃく ) me!" you slur, suffering from the effects of the tofu. "None of you cyan myake me go home! You cyan’t myake me! Nyah!" Hints Say this out loud, it'll help you remember. Really focus on the "myake" be sure to say it like you're all bugged out from tofu overdose.

meaningMnemonic: You're loiter ing, staring down at the cross that got caught in the net of your heart , because it's trying to teach you to act with virtue . Hints People who keep the cross in their hearts are supposed to be full of virtue, always doing the right thing, always helping others. But you aren't sure if you want to be virtuous, it's a lot of responsibility. So you look down at this symbolic cross and loiter instead of making a decision.
readingMnemonic: As you try to decide if you want to live a life of virtue the ghost of Toku gawa ( とく ) Ieyasu appears before you. He points to your heart and the cross, then points to his own and you see a glowing cross in his own. Hints I don't know about you, but I'm pretty sure Tokugawa Ieyasu is telling you to choose a life of virtue.

meaningMnemonic: The warehouse radical and the warehouse kanji are the same! You can call it a storehouse too. Hints Know your radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: You have a warehouse to store all of your sou ls ( そう ). When people or animals you know pass away, you take their souls and store them in your dry warehouse for safekeeping. It's a public service, really. Hints Imagine if you kept a bunch of souls in a warehouse. This way they can't haunt anyone. And they can't get lost out in the spirit world. The warehouse is best for them.

meaningMnemonic: Something that's plentiful and rich is abundant , plentiful and rich .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi of both kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 新しい社員には豊富な経験があります。
sentences.english: The new employee has abundant experience.

sentences.japanese: 人参にはベータカロテンが豊富に含まれている。
sentences.english: Carrots are a rich source of beta-carotene.

sentences.japanese: この店は品ぞろえが豊富です。
sentences.english: This store has a wide selection of items.

meaningMnemonic: Look for something. Research answers. This is an academic inquiry , or in other words, research .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 探究心を持ち続けることが、成長のカギです。
sentences.english: Continuing to have an inquisitive mind is the key to growth.

sentences.japanese: どうすれば効率よく漢字やボキャブラリーが習得できるのかを探究して出来上がったのがワニカニです。
sentences.english: WaniKani was created through researching how to learn kanji and vocabulary efficiently.

sentences.japanese: 探究を通じてのみ、私たちは新しい可能性と視点を発見することができるんです。
sentences.english: Only through inquiry can we discover new possibilities and perspectives.

sentences.japanese: 本書は私の宗教の探究、すなわち真理の探究の記録である。
sentences.english: This book documents my research into religion, that is, a record of the search for truth.

meaningMnemonic: An aviation ( 航空 ) ticket is the kind of ticket you need to fly on an airplane. That's an airplane ticket .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 航空券を予約しました。
sentences.english: I booked a plane ticket.

sentences.japanese: 航空券ってなんでこんなに高いの？
sentences.english: Why are plane tickets so expensive?

sentences.japanese: 博多までの航空券を手配してもらえますか。
sentences.english: Could you arrange a flight for me to Hakata?

sentences.japanese: 航空券をなくしたうえに、パスポートを犬に食べられたんです。
sentences.english: Not only did I lose my plane ticket, but my passport was eaten by my dog.

meaningMnemonic: Something that previously happened has already happened. 既に is relatively formal. Use it as a neutral way to describe actions or states that are already complete. By comparison, もう is more casual and might sometimes carry a sense of surprise or regret that something has happened sooner than expected.
readingMnemonic: The reading is different from what you learned with the kanji. But as I told you already , I'll be there on Su-day ( すで ). It's like Sunday, but not quite the same. Imagine your confusion when someone says this over and over, but you don't know what Suday is.

sentences.japanese: 既に支払いは完了しています。
sentences.english: The payment has already been completed.

sentences.japanese: この件について、部長には既に一言伝えてあります。
sentences.english: I have already mentioned this matter to the department manager.

sentences.japanese: 会議は既に始まっていますので、急いで参加してください。
sentences.english: The meeting has already started, so please hurry and join.

sentences.japanese: 私が電話した時、彼は既に退社してしまってました。
sentences.english: He had already left his office when I called him.

meaningMnemonic: I'm so surprised that it caused me to sigh . This is like when you see something super impressive and it surprises the heck out of you. Then, you breathe out a sigh because of your great amazement and admiration for what you just saw. 驚嘆 is a formal word you'll mostly see in writing to describe something truly awe-inspiring, or the state of being amazed by an impressive thing. It's about more than just surprise — it describes the deep admiration you feel when marveling at great talent, skill, or beauty.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: When a model human determine s something, that's an appraisal you should probably pay attention to. This isn't just some random nobody off the street — they're a model determiner, so they're really giving you an expert judgment . 鑑定 often refers to evaluating the authenticity or value of things like art, antiques, or real estate. It's also used in contexts like fingerprint analysis, or in legal settings where court-appointed experts provide technical evaluations to help judges make decisions.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

meaningMnemonic: " Use your heart and this pole when you guard me," you tell your bodyguard . A good bodyguard needs both — the heart of a lion, and a nice sturdy pole to smack fools with. 用心 actually means "caution," so 用心棒 suggests someone who watches out for danger — often with a 棒 (stick) in hand! The word has a bit of an old-school, samurai-era feel, but it still gets used both in writing and conversation from time to time.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji means showy , and this word is basically a super positive version of that — it means bright and showy . 華やか describes the kind of elegant beauty that brightens a room. A little showy, maybe, but in an uplifting way rather than just gaudy. It can describe gorgeous clothes, like 華やかなドレス (a gorgeous dress) or bright, festive colors and atmospheres.
readingMnemonic: For the reading, think about something that's bright and showy ... in particular, 花 s ( はな ). Flowers are super showy, always showing off their colors and stuff.

meaningMnemonic: Remember how the kanji could also mean city ? Well, that's what the vocab means too: the city . 街 refers to the general idea of an urban area , rather than a city as an official administrative unit. Compared to 町 , it suggests a bigger scale and a busier, more urban feel — places with shops, streets, and activity, like a にぎやかな街 (lively city) or 東京の街を歩く (walk the city streets of Tokyo).
readingMnemonic: Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it's going to use the kun'yomi reading, which you haven't learned yet. Lucky for you, 街 uses the same reading as another word you know for a place where people live: 町 ( まち ). Whether you're in a rural town or in the heart of the city , there's only one reading you need to remember. Pretty convenient, right?

meaningMnemonic: When the streets line up , they create a cityscape . 街並み usually refers to a developed, urban cityscape — imagine rows of buildings and shops with a lively, bustling feel. It can also be used for specific streetscape s, often with a distinct atmosphere or some kind of historical or cultural significance, like ヨーロッパの街並み (a European streetscape). You'll also see it written as 町並み , but this version tends to be used for quieter, more residential townscapes — often with a slightly sleepy, nostalgic vibe.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji means storehouse , and the vocab is also storehouse ! Wondering what the difference between 倉 and 庫 is? Long ago, 倉 were places to store grain, while 庫 used to be associated with places to store vehicles, as the kanji composition suggests. These days, they're both used for general storage, but also refer to places to store goods and merchandise. Between the two, 倉 is much more commonly used.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means detach , but what happens when something detaches? It causes it to become separated , aka to separate or to move away from something else. You use 離れる when two things that were together separate and become distant from one another. This can refer to a physical detachment, but it can also describe someone moving away from a place, group, or role, or even people drifting apart emotionally. You also use it to describe places that are far from each other.
readingMnemonic: For the reading, think about what it means to be separated . Imagine how all the cherry blossom 花 s ( はな ) separate from their branches and fall to the ground after blooming in the spring. Ah, to separate is so sad, and yet so beautiful!

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. This is an intransitive verb, meaning that it happens on its own, and we're not talking about what makes it happen. So this verb means to be extended , to be delayed , or to be prolonged . If you know the word ビル , you can think about how building work is always prolonged or delayed, to help you remember that this is intransitive. We never know why it's delayed, it just happens all by itself!
readingMnemonic: Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to be the kun'yomi reading. Lucky for you, the kanji readings for transitive and intransitive verbs are almost always the same. Once you learn one, you know them both! This reading is the same as 延ばす .

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means scatter so the verb vocab version is to be scattered or to get scattered . 散る is an intransitive verb, meaning something is scattering on its own. It's commonly used to describe when things like petals or leaves fall, fluttering down and scattering across the ground. It can also be used more abstractly, such as a crowd suddenly dispersing, your concentration breaking, your dreams falling apart, or even a soldier "falling" in battle. You know 散る is intransitive because you rue ( る ) your decision not to go see the cherry blossoms when they were in bloom; now the petals have all scattered to the wind and you've missed your chance. Darn.

sentences.japanese: 雨の日を除けば、毎日散歩している。
sentences.english: I go for a walk every day, except when it rains.

sentences.japanese: 赤い紙を除く全ての紙を、その折り目まで折ってください。
sentences.english: Fold all the papers, excluding the red one, to meet the crease.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means fear so the verb version is to fear .
readingMnemonic: The reading is shared with 恐ろしい , which is "scary." Use that, and don't be afraid. You'll be able to learn this reading yet.

sentences.japanese: 失敗を恐れてばかりいては前に進めないよ。
sentences.english: You can't move forward if you always fear failure.

sentences.japanese: 目が見えなくなること以外は、何も恐れることはないよ。
sentences.english: I'm not afraid of anything except for going blind.

sentences.japanese: 私たちは変化を恐れずに、どんどん新しいことにチャレンジしていくべきです。
sentences.english: We should not fear change and should continue to challenge ourselves with new things.

sentences.japanese: コウイチは自分の力を恐れているんですよ。
sentences.english: Koichi fears his own power.

meaningMnemonic: 緊張 means "nervousness" or "tension." So, the verb version is to feel nervous or to get tense . People often use 緊張する when they're about to do something important, like giving a speech or taking a test. In formal contexts it can also be used to talk about muscles physically getting tense.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.japanese: 試合前に緊張するのはよくあることです。
sentences.english: It's common to get nervous before a match.

sentences.japanese: 初めてのデートで緊張した。
sentences.english: I was nervous on my first date.

sentences.japanese: 緊張しすぎて、手がふるえました。
sentences.english: I was so nervous that my hands started shaking.

sentences.japanese: 大事なプレゼンなので、とても緊張しています。
sentences.english: I'm very nervous for an important presentation.

meaningMnemonic: If 主催 means "host" or "hosting," the verb version of that would be to host . 主催する refers to hosting events, especially formal ones like conferences, concerts, or company parties. It's not just about "doing" an event — it shows that the person or group is the main sponsor and organizer, the one really in charge of making it happen.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. It will help to know the word 主催 already as well.

sentences.japanese: このイベントは市が主催するものです。
sentences.english: This event is hosted by the city.

sentences.japanese: うちの学校で土曜日にカラオケパーティーを主催するんだけど、よかったら来ない？
sentences.english: Our school is hosting a karaoke party this Saturday. Would you like to join us?

sentences.japanese: ワニカニが漢字合宿を主催したら、参加してくれるユーザーさんはどれくらいいると思いますか？
sentences.english: How many users do you think would join if WaniKani hosted a kanji boot camp?

sentences.japanese: 近所のおばあちゃんたちがビンゴ大会を主催してくれたんだけど、一位の景品は金の入れ歯でした。
sentences.english: Some elderly ladies in the neighborhood hosted a bingo tournament, and the first prize was gold dentures.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means illuminate , so this means to illuminate or to shine light on something. But don't get it confused with 照れる , which is "to feel embarrassed" — that would be embarrassing. You know this is "to illuminate" because you get a rash ( らす ) every time something shines on you too much.
readingMnemonic: Speaking of things that illuminate, your hand s ( 手 ) illuminate all the time for some reason.

sentences.japanese: 僕にとって、あなたは黒い海を照らしてくれる月のような存在です。
sentences.english: To me, you are like the moon that illuminates the black sea.

sentences.japanese: 君はこのシーンで、スポットライトでこの花を照らすんだ。
sentences.english: In this scene, you'll be shining the spotlight on the flower.

sentences.japanese: 法律に照らして、このツイートが適切かどうかを確認しましょう。
sentences.english: We will check if this tweet is appropriate in the light of the law.

sentences.japanese: ちょっとスマホのライトであそこの方を照らしてくれない？
sentences.english: Can you shine your phone's flashlight over there for a sec?

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means inquire so the verb vocab version is to inquire , or simply to ask . 尋ねる is the polite, slightly formal word you use when you directly ask someone for information you don't know — like directions or details.
readingMnemonic: You want to inquire about some serious matters, but Taz ( たず ), your Tasmanian Devil friend, keeps interrupting to ask silly questions instead.

sentences.japanese: これは彼に直接尋ねるのが一番早いと思います。
sentences.english: As for this, I think the quickest way is to ask him directly.

sentences.japanese: 人に尋ねる前に、まずは自分で調べてみてください。
sentences.english: Please try researching it yourself before asking others.

sentences.japanese: お店の営業時間を尋ねるつもりだったが、誰もいなかった。
sentences.english: I was going to ask about the store hours, but there was no one there.

sentences.japanese: 何を尋ねても、夫はいつも逃げるような答えを返すばかりで…のれんに腕押しってやつですよ。
sentences.english: No matter what I ask, my husband always gives evasive answers... it's like talking to a brick wall.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means knit so the verb vocab version is to knit .
readingMnemonic: When you start to knit , you always end up with the same thing every time when you're done, no matter what you're trying to make: The letter " A " ( あ ). It's so frustrating that you can't knit anything else.

sentences.japanese: 母が私のためにマフラーを編んでくれた。
sentences.english: My mom knitted a scarf for me.

sentences.japanese: 私の父は、セーターを編むのがとても上手だった。
sentences.english: My dad was really good at knitting sweaters.

sentences.japanese: ブラジャーを編んでみようと思ったきっかけはなんですか。
sentences.english: What inspired you to knit bras?

sentences.japanese: ある朝、目が覚めると、おばあちゃんがコタツで、だまって黒い手ぶくろを編んでいた。
sentences.english: One morning, when I woke up, my grandmother was silently knitting a pair of black gloves at the kotatsu.

meaningMnemonic: This is one of those words that makes more sense when you look at the reading. The "Virtue River" isn't some virtuous river, it's in fact the Tokugawa family name, made famous by the Tokugawa shogunate. They ran Japan for a while, you know?
readingMnemonic: The readings are 徳 and the vocab 川 put together into one word. Once you can read this, you'll know the meaning too, so focus on the reading for this one. Just watch out for the rendaku that changes かわ to がわ !

sentences.japanese: 徳川家康って誰？
sentences.english: Who is Tokugawa Ieyasu?

sentences.japanese: うちの犬、徳川家っぽい顔してると思わない？
sentences.english: Doesn't my dog kind of look like someone from the Tokugawa family?

sentences.japanese: 徳川の時代にもどりたいって言ったら、ママにスマホ取り上げられた。
sentences.english: When I said I wanted to go back to the Tokugawa era, Mom took away my smartphone.

sentences.japanese: 彼女は歴女で、徳川幕府にはとても精通しています。
sentences.english: She's a history nerd, and she's very knowledgeable about the Tokugawa Shogunate.

meaningMnemonic: The virtue island prefecture is Tokushima prefecture . The reading will give away the meaning of this one, so long as you knew "prefecture."
readingMnemonic: The readings are the ones you learned with the individual kanji. Put them together and you'll know this is Tokushima Prefecture .

sentences.japanese: 徳島県にはまだ行ったことがないけど、いつか行ってみたいんだよね。
sentences.english: I haven't been to Tokushima yet, but I'd love to visit someday.

sentences.japanese: 徳島県の観光パンフレットを駅でもらいました。
sentences.english: I picked up a tourism pamphlet for Tokushima at the station.

sentences.english: I was surprised that Tokushima was more urban than I expected.

sentences.japanese: 知事は、徳島県をどういう風に変えていくおつもりですか？私は今のままがいいと思うのですが。
sentences.english: Governor, in what ways would you change Tokushima Prefecture? I think I like things just the way they are.

meaningMnemonic: When you sigh , you feel a certain type of emotion. A type that makes you feel sad and causes you to lament and to grieve .
readingMnemonic: For the reading, just think about this feeling you're having (this lamenting grieving one). Then, decide you're done with it. 投げ る (throw) it out the window. You don't want these feels anymore!

sentences.japanese: 自分の運命を嘆くのは、そろそろやめにしないか？
sentences.english: Isn't it about time you stopped lamenting your fate?

sentences.japanese: 彼は貧乏を嘆くのではなく、努力した。だからこそ、成功したのだ。
sentences.english: He didn't lament his poverty; instead, he worked hard. That's exactly why he succeeded.

sentences.japanese: 私は、毎日同じ服を着ている理由を誰も聞いてくれないことを嘆いた。
sentences.english: I lamented that no one ever asked why I wore the same clothes every day.

sentences.japanese: どんなにくよくよ嘆いていても、時間はもどらないんだから、嘆くのはやめて前に進もうよ！
sentences.english: No matter how much you grieve, time won't turn back, so let's stop worrying and move forward!

meaningMnemonic: You learned 迷う means "to go astray," and 迷わす is its transitive version, meaning it takes a direct object. So it means to lead someone astray , to perplex someone , or to mislead someone . While 迷わす can mean literally causing someone to get lost, it's more commonly used for the act of confusing someone — for example, overwhelming them with difficult choices or intentionally misleading them in a malicious way. You know this verb is transitive because there's nothing worse ( わす ) than purposefully misleading someone. Intentionally leading someone astray is worse than anything!
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 迷う , so use that so you aren't lead astray too.

sentences.japanese: ごめん、迷わすつもりじゃなかったんだけど…。
sentences.english: Sorry, I didn't mean to lead you astray…

sentences.japanese: 相手を迷わすような発言はしないようにすべきだ。
sentences.english: You should avoid saying things that mislead others.

sentences.japanese: 人々を迷わすために、あえて間違った看板が立てられているんだよ。
sentences.english: They deliberately put up false signs to lead people astray.

sentences.japanese: もし俺の娘を路頭に迷わすようなことがあったら、一生許さないぞ。
sentences.english: If you lead my daughter astray, I'll never forgive you.

meanings: To Put An End To Something
meaningMnemonic: Remember how 絶える means "to die out?" Well 絶やす is its transitive version, meaning to let something die out or to put an end to something . 絶やす is used when you stop something from continuing, like ending a family line, letting a tradition fade, or allowing a fire to go out. You know this because if you're putting an end to something, you probably don't like it, so you say " YAASS " ( やす ) with a big evil grin as you let it die out. Note that 絶やす often appears in its negative form 絶やさない , because it's commonly used to describe the intent not to let something precious or important come to an end.
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 絶える .

sentences.english: never stop smiling, always keep a smile

sentences.japanese: 火を絶やさない
sentences.english: not let the fire go out

sentences.japanese: 伝統を絶やさない
sentences.english: not let traditions die out

sentences.japanese: 子孫を絶やさない
sentences.english: never let the family line end

sentences.japanese: 彼女はいつも笑顔を絶やすことがなかった。
sentences.english: She never let her smile die out.

sentences.english: Make sure the fire doesn't go out during the night.

sentences.japanese: 今にも消えそうな命を絶やさないために、彼はピザを注文した。
sentences.english: To keep his nearly-vanishing life from being extinguished, he ordered a pizza.

sentences.japanese: 日本の伝統を絶やしてはなりません。どうすれば私たちの文化を守ることができるのか、共に考えてください。
sentences.english: We must not let Japan's traditions fade. Please think with me about how we can protect our culture.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means look for and the verb version of the kanji is to look for . Curious about the difference between 捜す and 探す ? While there is some overlap between the two, 捜す is typically used in official, thorough searches for something or someone that is thought to concretely exist and has disappeared or cannot be easily found. In contrast, 探す can also be used for personal searches for things that one desires or is looking for.
readingMnemonic: You are looking for a sagger ( さが ) amongst the products you're shipping off overseas. The saggers are the boxes that have weird lumps sagging out of them, which means they broke and are getting things wet. So, find the saggers. Go to search for them, because they could ruin the whole shipment.

sentences.english: I looked for the remote for ten minutes. It was in the toaster.

sentences.japanese: 三本足の犬がバーにやって来てこう言った。「俺の足を撃った男を探しているんだ。半分河豚で半分豆腐みたいな男なんだが。」
sentences.english: A three legged dog walked into a bar and said, "I'm searching for the man who shot my paw. He looks like half fugu and half tofu."

meaningMnemonic: 結婚 means "marriage," so the verb version of that would be to marry or to get married .
readingMnemonic: You've already learned 結婚 , so you should be okay here. As with that word, watch out for 結 's けつ reading changing to けっ .

sentences.english: to marry a salaried worker

sentences.english: Those two got married last year.

sentences.japanese: 俺、彼女と結婚するつもりなんだ。
sentences.english: I intend to marry her.

sentences.japanese: 結婚するなら、ちゃんと色々と考えた方がいいよ。
sentences.english: If you're going to get married, there are a lot of things you ought to think about first.

sentences.japanese: お前、もう元カノについて考えるのはよした方がいいぞ。特に、サーモンのお父さんに彼女と結婚していいかどうか聞いて、許しも得ちまったんだからな。
sentences.english: You've gotta stop thinking about your ex-girlfriend, man — especially since you already asked Salmon's dad if you could marry her and got his permission.

meaningMnemonic: You learned that 積もる (to accumulate) is used when something like snow or dust piles up over time. 積む is the transitive version, so it means to pile something up , to stack up , or to load . You know this because you are the one mo ving ( む ) things to pile them up! 積む is often used for physical actions like stacking boxes or loading luggage, but it's also used in more abstract ways, such as building up experience or skills. Think of it like "stacking up" experience points to level up in your life!
readingMnemonic: The reading comes from 積もる , so pile up your knowledge and remember it that way.

sentences.japanese: 荷物を積むのに少し時間がかかるから、そこで待ってて！
sentences.english: It will take a little time to load the luggage, so wait there!

sentences.english: His "to-be-read" list had many books piled up.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means resemble so the verb vocab version is to resemble or to look like .
readingMnemonic: You should have learned this reading with the kanji, but here's a mnemonic to help you, just in case: What are you trying to resemble ?? Is that... oh no. A knee ( に ) face resemble surgery, where you make your face look like your knee and vice versa? Do you know how dangerous that surgery is?

sentences.japanese: このズボン、私がずっと探してたズボンに似てる。
sentences.english: These pants look like the ones I've been trying to find for a while.

sentences.japanese: 長く付き合うカップルは顔が似てくることが多い。
sentences.english: Couples who have been together for a long time often end up looking alike.

sentences.japanese: 最初はお母さんに似ていると思っていたけど、だんだんお父さんにも似てきたね！

sentences.english: Isn't it unlikely that they look this similar by coincidence? I think it's fair if people call it a rip-off.

meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means savings , so the verb vocab version means to save up , to store , or to accumulate something valuable. 貯める is used when you're saving up something useful over time — typically money, loyalty points, or airline miles, for example, but sometimes water and other resources too.
readingMnemonic: This word uses the kun'yomi reading for 貯 , which you haven't learned yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you out: You have to save up for ta cos ( た ). Not only are tacos more expensive these days, you also have a horrible taco addiction that you need to plan ahead and save for every month.

sentences.english: to save up over several years

sentences.english: Japanese people really love collecting reward points, don't they?

meaningMnemonic: You learned 詰める means "to stuff in." When you want to see something so much that you "stuff" your gaze into it, you're probably going to stare at it. 見詰める means to gaze at something intently, often with deep thought, admiration, curiosity, or strong emotions. Keep in mind that you'll usually see this word with the 詰 in kana, as 見つめる .
readingMnemonic: The reading is 見 and 詰める .

sentences.japanese: 好きな人をこっそり見詰めるのって、青春っぽいよね。
sentences.english: Secretly staring at your crush—so youthful, isn't it?

sentences.english: The dog was staring intently at the balloon flying straight up, higher and higher.

meaningMnemonic: Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means sweep so the verb version is to sweep .
readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you: Whenever you have to sweep something, you end up getting way too into it: " Hah ( は )! Take that dirt! Hah! Think you can hang out on my floor, dust? Think again! Hah!"

sentences.english: Sweeping the yard every morning is part of my routine.

sentences.english: He prefers sweeping with a broom rather than using a vacuum cleaner.

sentences.english: Could you sweep the meeting room before the meeting starts?

sentences.japanese: ゴミを掃きながら気づいたんだけど、ほうきって意外といいストレッチになるかも。
sentences.english: I realized while sweeping the trash that a broom might actually make for a good stretch.

meaningMnemonic: If 催促 is urge , then the verb version would be to urge .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well. Will help to know 催促 first.

sentences.japanese: バナナを催促するゴリラの顔が忘れられない。
sentences.english: I can't forget the face of the gorilla urging for a banana.

sentences.english: I'm sorry to be so demanding, but can you take some pictures of Tokyo Tower and send them to me by Monday please? Thanks.

meaningMnemonic: The normal steps are the ones that are totally usual . They're the ones you usually do, unlike those weird not usual steps.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.english: I apologized to my mother for not calling her more regularly.

meaningMnemonic: A field vegetable is still a vegetable , whether it comes from the field or not.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 野菜をたっぷり使ったスープを作りました。
sentences.english: I made a soup full of vegetables.

sentences.japanese: スーパーで見切り品の野菜を安く買えた。
sentences.english: I got discounted vegetables at the supermarket.

sentences.japanese: うちの子、「大きくなったら野菜になりたい」って言うんです。
sentences.english: My child says, "When I grow up, I want to become a vegetable."

sentences.japanese: どんなにお腹が苦しくても、野菜なら食べられます。
sentences.english: No matter how full I am, I can eat vegetables.

meaningMnemonic: If you eat vegetable food you are on a vegetarian diet .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: 彼女は菜食主義者です。
sentences.english: She is a vegetarian.

sentences.japanese: 夕食はできるだけ菜食するようにしています。
sentences.english: I try to be on a vegetable diet for dinner as much as possible.

sentences.japanese: 菜食生活、ちょっと憧れるかも。
sentences.english: I kind of admire the vegetarian lifestyle.

sentences.japanese: 菜食の生活を続けてもう三年になりますが、時々無性に焼肉が食べたくなる時があります。
sentences.english: I have been on a vegetarian diet for three years already, but sometimes I have an irresistible craving for yakiniku.

meaningMnemonic: A storage warehouse is some kind of warehouse , or some kind of storehouse . Curious about the difference between 倉庫 and 庫 ? While 庫 refers to traditional Japanese storehouses, 倉庫 is used for modern warehouses and storehouses (both the commercial and personal kind).
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: あの倉庫、今は誰も使っていないはずだよ。
sentences.english: That warehouse shouldn't be in use by anyone right now.

sentences.japanese: 倉庫に入ったら、タイムマシンがあったんだよ。
sentences.english: I walked into a warehouse and found a time machine.

sentences.japanese: これは、倉庫にコウイチと二人で閉じ込められた時にプレイしたカードゲームです。
sentences.english: This is the card game I played with Koichi when the two of us were trapped in the warehouse.

sentences.japanese: 倉庫の鍵を閉めるには、カチッという音が聞こえるまでレバーを上げる必要があります。
sentences.english: You need to lift the lever until you hear a click to lock the warehouse.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are almost exactly the same. Someone who is rich has wealth and riches , right?
readingMnemonic: For the reading, think about the person you know with the most wealth . It is Tommy ( とみ ) Hilfiger.

sentences.japanese: 富と力
sentences.english: wealth and power

sentences.japanese: 富と名声
sentences.english: wealth and fame

sentences.japanese: 富と権力
sentences.english: wealth and power

sentences.japanese: 莫大な富
sentences.english: enormous wealth

sentences.japanese: 富の集中
sentences.english: concentration of wealth

sentences.japanese: 富の象徴
sentences.english: symbols of wealth

sentences.japanese: 富の分配
sentences.english: distribution of wealth

sentences.japanese: 世界の富
sentences.english: the wealth of the world

sentences.japanese: 巨万の富
sentences.english: great riches

sentences.japanese: 巨額の富
sentences.english: great riches

sentences.japanese: 富をもたらす
sentences.english: to bring riches

sentences.japanese: 富を得る
sentences.english: to acquire wealth

sentences.japanese: 富を生み出す
sentences.english: to create wealth

sentences.japanese: 昔は名声も富も得たいと思っていましたが、今得たいのは富だけですね。
sentences.english: In the past, I wanted to gain both fame and wealth, but now all I want to gain is wealth.

sentences.japanese: 富をもたらすのは、お金だけじゃないよ。真の富は、心が豊かになることで感じるものだからね。
sentences.english: It is not just money that brings wealth. True wealth is something felt when the heart becomes rich.

sentences.japanese: 巨万の富を築くことは思ったより簡単ではありません。
sentences.english: Making a fortune of millions is not as easy as I thought.

sentences.japanese: 世界の富の９割は、実はクラビゲーター教団を構成する少数の権力者たちが持っていると言われている。
sentences.english: They say that 90% of the world's wealth is actually in the possession of a small group of powerful people who make up the Cult of the Crabigator.

meaningMnemonic: If you're rich and abundant , you are super wealthy , affluent , and rich .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: モルディブは富裕層の間で人気の高いリゾート地です。
sentences.english: The Maldives is a highly popular resort destination among the wealthy class.

sentences.japanese: 富裕な家庭出身のあなたには分からないでしょうね。
sentences.english: Coming from a wealthy family, you wouldn't understand.

sentences.japanese: ワニカニには少数の富裕者だけがアクセスできるエリートクラブ的なコンテンツがあると聞いたのですが、本当ですか？
sentences.english: I heard that WaniKani has elite club-like content accessible only to a small number of wealthy individuals. Is that true?

sentences.japanese: どうして人は富裕層と貧困層に分けられるのでしょうか。
sentences.english: Why do we separate people into the rich and the poor?

meaningMnemonic: This earth belt is the area within the belt, which holds this area of earth in. It is separate from the rest of the earth, making it its own zone or district .
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

sentences.japanese: ここは、あなた以外には安全地帯です。
sentences.english: This is a safe zone for everyone but you.

sentences.japanese: この地域は農業地帯で、広い畑が広がっています。
sentences.english: This region is an agricultural zone, with vast fields stretching out.

sentences.japanese: 産業地帯では、工場が立ち並んでおり、多くの人が働いています。
sentences.english: In the industrial zone, factories line the streets, and many people work there.

sentences.japanese: 新しい道路が開通すると、この地帯のアクセスが改善されます。
sentences.english: When the new road opens, access to this zone will be improved.
